title: Black composers in Hollywood and bringing Oliver Nelson out
summary: Carter notes more black composers now work in Hollywood and recounts recommending Oliver Nelson for a Universal job.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: Uh huh. We talked earlier about the very few black musicians and composers working in Hollywood, and in the early 40's when you came. That, of course, has changed somewhat. I mean, there are some more.
Yes, it's changed quite a bit.
Who are some of those people who have come since your time ... since your first ...

Well, I guess notably, Quincy Jones; that's the first one the pops into my mind. First name. Gee, Quincy ... I don't know when he came; he did "The Pawnbroker" -- I don't know what year that was. But up to now, he's done over 30 films, you know.
Oliver Nelson has done a few films, and a great number of TV shows.

JJ. Johnson has ... actually, JJ. Johnson is now doing "The Six Million Dollar Man" which, you know ... he has taken over on that. After Oliver Nelson passed away. Last year. And Benny Golson, we must remember, too.

And you saw all these people coming in? I mean, they came in while you were there. Did they -- did their work begin with one film, usually -- how did they break in? I mean, what was the process? Did they come there for one particular purpose -- with a contract already in their hands, or did they just come there and say, well, "Here I am. I'm gonna try to get some work in the studios."?
Well, I don't know about the others, but I know how Oliver Nelson came there, and I don't want to give any undue credit to myself, because it's not

why I'm telling you this, but when I was working at Universal, I was asked to look at a picture for a producer, and I looked at the picture and he said that he wanted a score like an album that he was going to play for me. And he played an album for me, and it was, I believe it was a Jimmy Smith album, that had been done by Oliver Nelson.

So he wanted this kind of music -- wanted to know could I do this. Well, at the time, I was very, very busy anyway, doing other things, and I would have kind of had to cram to get that in my then busy schedule.

So I knew that they had, you know, brought composers from as far away as Paris and London to do just a TV episode, you know? And I said, 'Well, gee, this is done by Oliver Nelson --why don't you try to get him to come and do this segment for you. When does it have to be done? If this is the music that you really want; if it's that important to you, get the man who does it so well.' You know.
And so they thought this was a good idea, but wanted to know did I think he would come. I said, 'Well, all you can do is contact him.'
And I helped him get in touch with him, and Oliver agreed to come and do it, and once he came, they liked his work.
And he liked it, and that was it.
